The matrix $A$ above has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=5$ and $\lambda_2=-8.$ Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $D=P^T \! A P.$
examples.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PDP^T,
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D=P^TAP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Note that $A$ is symmetric. Therefore, it is orthogonally diagonalizable. Let's now go through the process.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we already have the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=5\quad$ and $\quad \lambda_2=-8$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For $\lambda_1=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 6 \\ 6 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14075254/assets/7b0367066950407149521e6b06255f71b25fe5e67bc609fac5e914d3d1315fe7.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{13},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14075254/assets/498ecfed1cfe5ed4b1df8c02088045e67c4d5601e47f403288d271447c5ded28.png)

- For $\lambda_2=-8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-8)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]+8[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-8)I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14075254/assets/0aa3aecabd941ccc8e176aef479eb3630197ff9c7fb6ca63e028e41315c9aafb.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{13},$ we get

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 \\ 6 & -1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=8$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5.$ So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-5.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=-5.$ Computing $A-(-5)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+5I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 \\ 6 & -1\end{aligned}]+5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=-3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{13}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm, we obtain the second column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2\sqrt{13}}{13} \\ -\frac{3\sqrt{13}}{13}\end{aligned}]
$$
